title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Introduction to Quarto
Quarto lets data scientists write reports, slide decks, and papers as plain-text documents that combine writing, code, and results. When the data or the analysis changes, you re-render, and every number, figure, and table updates itself. This book is a hands-on introduction, built around a single running example: 170 years of ice records for Lake Mendota, which grow from an empty file into a published report, a slide deck, and a paper.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
How this book is organized
The book has two parts.
Basic has five units, covered live in a one-hour, hands-on workshop. They follow the life of a typical project: a report, then slides for a talk, then a paper.

Unit 1 introduces Quarto and how it turns a .qmd file into a finished document.
Units 2–3 build a report and publish it online.
Units 4–5 reuse that report to make a slide deck and a paper.

Advanced units go beyond the live hour and are for you to work through on your own afterward. They pick up where the workshop leaves off, using the same report.qmd, slides.qmd, and paper.qmd you built. To see what a new feature does, add it to your own file and render it (or publish it) yourself.

Git with Quarto projects: which Quarto files to commit and which to ignore. Start here, so the work you did in the workshop is safely committed before you experiment.
Advanced markdown: more ways to format text, including links, images, tables, math, and callouts.
Chunk options and figures: control what each code chunk shows, and size, caption, and arrange figures.
Tables: turn data frames into tables that look good in HTML, Word, and PDF.
Advanced slide formatting: columns, themes, code on slides, and more for your decks.
YAML in depth: more settings for reports, decks, and papers, and where YAML can live.
Quarto projects and paths: what a _quarto.yml file does, and how your code finds its files.
Reusing code across products: keep one copy of your analysis code for a report, slides, and a paper.

Each Basic unit also has a companion slide deck, published on Posit Connect Cloud. These are the decks we present live. The Advanced units are in the book only.



Unit
Slide deck




1 — What Is Quarto?
open deck


2 — Your First Quarto Report
open deck


3 — Render and Publish
open deck


4 — Slide Decks
open deck


5 — Writing a Paper
open deck





Before the workshop
Please finish these steps before the workshop so we can spend our time together on Quarto itself. They take about 15 minutes.
This setup builds on the Git workshop. It assumes you already have:

Git installed (on Windows, this gave you Git Bash)
A GitHub account
An SSH key connecting your computer to GitHub

Type every command below in a terminal: Terminal on macOS or Linux, Git Bash on Windows, or the terminal inside RStudio.

Step 1: Install Quarto
Download the installer for your operating system from https://quarto.org/docs/download/ and run it.
RStudio comes with its own copy of Quarto, but please install Quarto separately anyway. The separate install works in any terminal, and it lets you control which version you have. You won’t break anything: RStudio will use your installed copy automatically.
When the installer finishes, close any open terminals and restart RStudio so they can find Quarto.


Step 2: Check your Quarto version
Open a new terminal and run:
quarto --version
You need version 1.9 or higher. Earlier versions can’t publish to Posit Connect Cloud from the terminal, which we will do in the workshop.
If you don’t see a version number of 1.9 or higher:

command not found: Quarto isn’t installed, or the terminal can’t find it yet. Re-run the installer, then open a new terminal and try again.
A version lower than 1.9: your terminal is finding an older copy of Quarto, often one installed for an earlier course. Run which quarto to see where that copy lives. Then download the current installer from the link above, run it, and check the version again in a new terminal.

For a fuller diagnosis, quarto check reports which version of Quarto you are running and whether it can find R and Python.


Step 3: Create a Posit Connect Cloud account
Posit Connect Cloud is a free service for sharing documents online. We will publish a report and a slide deck to it during the workshop.

Go to https://connect.posit.cloud/
Click Sign Up
Choose to sign up with GitHub, using the GitHub account you already have

The free plan is all you need. If you already have an account, you can skip this step.


Step 4: Create your workshop repo on GitHub
During the workshop you will build a small project about ice cover on Lake Mendota. Make a home for it on GitHub now.
In your browser, signed in to GitHub:

Click + (top right) → New repository
Name it mendota_ice
Choose Public or Private; either works
From the Add .gitignore dropdown, choose the R template
Click Create repository

Don’t skip the .gitignore. It tells Git to ignore the clutter that R and RStudio create (like .Rhistory and .Rproj.user/). It also gives the repo its first commit, so when you clone it, git push and git pull work right away.


Step 5: Clone the repo to your computer
On your new repo’s page, click the green Code button, select the SSH tab, and copy the address.
In your terminal, move to the folder where you keep your GitHub repos. We used ~/github in the Git workshop; use your own folder if it’s different. Then clone the repo, pasting your own address:
cd ~/github
git clone git@github.com:your_username/mendota_ice.git
Move into the new folder and look around:
cd mendota_ice
ls -a
.  ..  .git  .gitignore
You should see the .gitignore you created on GitHub, plus the hidden .git folder that holds the repo’s history.


Step 6: Download the data, references, and citation style
Our report will use 170 years of ice records for Lake Mendota, and our paper will cite them in APA style. Put a copy of the data in a data folder inside your repo. Put the reference file (refs.bib) and the APA style file (apa.csl) at the top of your repo.
Stay in your mendota_ice folder. Copy the four commands below (use the copy button at the top right of the box), paste them into your terminal, and press Enter:
mkdir data
curl -fsSL -o data/mendota_ice.csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jjcurtin/book_quarto/main/data/mendota_ice.csv
curl -fsSL -o refs.bib https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jjcurtin/book_quarto/main/refs.bib
curl -fsSL -o apa.csl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jjcurtin/book_quarto/main/apa.csl
mkdir makes the data folder. Each curl command downloads one file. If all goes well, none of the commands prints anything.
Check that the files arrived:
head -3 data/mendota_ice.csv
head -1 refs.bib
grep "<title>" apa.csl
winter,year,ice_days
1855-56,1856,118
1856-57,1857,151
@dataset{magnuson2026,
    <title>APA Style 7th edition</title>
If you see an error instead, make sure you are in your mendota_ice folder (pwd shows where you are), then paste the commands again. If mkdir says the folder already exists, that’s fine; just run the three curl lines.
That’s it. You’re ready for the workshop. We will start from this folder.



How to use this book
Quarto is best learned by doing. As you read, follow along in your own mendota_ice repo: write each file in RStudio (or any editor) and render it yourself. Everything builds one running example, so the report, slides, and paper you create grow right alongside the book.
We render and publish from the terminal (Terminal on macOS or Linux, Git Bash on Windows, or the terminal in RStudio), not with buttons in RStudio. The commands are short, they work the same in any editor, and you will see exactly what Quarto is doing.
A few conventions to know:

Commands you type appear in shaded code blocks, with the output shown just below them.
Your turn boxes are short challenges to try on your own before moving on.

The source for this book lives on GitHub; corrections and suggestions are welcome.

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.1 Why are we here?
By the end of this hour you will be able to:
You’ll build along with me the whole hour, with a few Your turn moments to try a step on your own.

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
Explain what Quarto is and how it works with R and RStudio
Write a report that mixes text and R code
Render it to a self-contained file and publish it online
Turn the same kind of document into a slide deck
Write a manuscript with citations and cross-references

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.2 What is Quarto?
Quarto is a free, open-source publishing system.



You write one plain-text file (a .qmd) that mixes:

Text, written in markdown
Code, in R or Python
A few options at the top, written in YAML




Quarto turns that file into a finished document:

Reports (HTML, Word, PDF)
Slide decks
Manuscripts and journal articles
Posters, websites, dashboards (these are not covered today)

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.3 R, RStudio, and Quarto
Three tools, three different jobs:











Tool
What it is
Its job




R (or Python)
A programming language
Runs your code: data, models, figures


RStudio
An IDE
Where you write code and documents


Quarto
A publishing system
Turns your .qmd into a finished document






You use them together:

write a .qmd in RStudio,
render it from the terminal, and
Quarto has R run your code and builds the document around the results.

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.4 What happens when you render
quarto render report.qmd






flowchart LR
  Q[".qmd<br/>text + code"] --> E["engine<br/>runs the code"]
  E --> M[".md<br/>text + results"]
  M --> P["Pandoc<br/>converts"]
  P --> O["HTML, Word,<br/>PDF, slides"]










An engine runs your code chunks: knitr for R, Jupyter for Python
Your numbers, tables, and figures are woven into the text
Pandoc converts the result to the format you asked for




The engine runs your code in a fresh session,

not in your RStudio console.
Remember this; it matters in the next unit.

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.5 Why use Quarto?







The old way
With Quarto




Copy numbers from the console into Word, then they drift out of date when the data change
Text and code live together; numbers are computed every time you render


Rebuild the same figure for the report, the slides, and the paper
One source, many formats


Type citations by hand and renumber figures when you reorder them
Citations come from a .bib file; figure and table numbers update themselves


“How did I get this result?”
Rendering re-runs everything from scratch, so the document is the record


Binary files that Git can’t compare
Plain text that works with Git

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.6 A few quick notes
Quarto is its own program.

Like Git, you run it from the terminal, and every command starts with quarto.
It works the same whether you edit in RStudio, Positron, VS Code, or Jupyter.




It is not just for R.

If your project uses Python, you can use Quarto the same way.
Code chunks just say {python} instead of {r}.




Coming from R Markdown?

Quarto is its successor.
Most of what you know carries over, and your .Rmd files still work.

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.7 Source vs. output











File
What it is
What you do with it




report.qmd
The source
Write and edit it; commit it to Git


report.html
The output
Read and share it; never edit it by hand






Quarto rebuilds the output from scratch every time you render, so any edits you make to the HTML will be overwritten.



To change the output, change the source and render again.

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.8 Where we are
We have:

Defined Quarto as a publishing system, separate from R and RStudio
Seen what happens when you render
Seen why it beats copy and paste for reports, slides, and papers











ImportantNext up



Time to write one. Next we will build our first Quarto report about a Madison favorite: ice on Lake Mendota.

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.1 When is Lake Mendota frozen?
The Wisconsin State Climatology Office decides each winter.
For Mendota, one of their rules is a bit unusual:
The story, handed down by oral tradition:

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
Can you row a boat from Picnic Point to Maple Bluff?
If not, the lake is frozen.






UW limnologists E. A. Birge and Chancey Juday were often out on the lake in a rowboat
The ice along that line decided whether they could row a case of beer to their friends in Maple Bluff

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.2 Our data
Observers have recorded ice on Lake Mendota every winter since the 1850s.



You downloaded them to data/mendota_ice.csv, one row per winter:

winter: the winter, e.g., 1855-56
year: the year that winter ended
ice_days: days the lake was frozen




171 winters, from 1855-56 to 2025-26.

The question for our report: is ice cover declining?

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.3 What we will build
One file, report.qmd, with:

A YAML header: title, author, date, format
Text written in markdown: headings, paragraphs, lists
Code chunks that load the data and draw a figure
Inline R: numbers in sentences, computed from the data




We will render it after each step so you can see what changed.

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.4 Create the file
In the terminal, move into your repo and create an empty file:
cd ~/github/mendota_ice
touch report.qmd



Then open report.qmd in RStudio:

Use the Files pane, or File → Open File
It is a plain-text file, like an .R script

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
section: 2.5 The YAML (“Yet Another Markup Language”) header
text:
2.5 The YAML (“Yet Another Markup Language”) header
Type this at the very top of report.qmd:
---
title: "Ice Cover on Lake Mendota"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format: html
---



The header sits between two lines of ---

Each line is a key: value pair
format: html says what to build
date: today fills in the date each time you render




Now save report.qmd (You can use the save button on the toolbar in RStudio)

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.6 Render it
Back in the terminal:
quarto render report.qmd



Quarto writes report.html next to your .qmd.

Open it in your browser
In RStudio: click it in the Files pane → View in Web Browser




So far, just a title, author, and date.

Each time you change the .qmd, render again and reload the page

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.7 Markdown: headings, text, and lists
Below the YAML header, add:
## Background

Lake Mendota has been watched for ice since the **1850s**.

For each winter, the record notes:

- the date the lake froze
- the date it opened

## Ice cover over time




## is a section heading, ### a subsection
Put a space after the #
Start at ##; the YAML title is already the top level
**bold** makes text bold
A line starting with - is a list item

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.8 Blank lines matter
If you leave out the blank line before the list (Don’t do this step today)
For each winter, the record notes:
- the date the lake froze
- the date it opened



You get one run-on paragraph:

For each winter, the record notes: - the date the lake froze - the date it opened




Markdown needs a blank line:

before a list
before and after a heading
between paragraphs

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.9 Your turn







ImportantTry it




Add the headings, text, and list from the last few slides
Save report.qmd
Render with quarto render report.qmd
Reload report.html and check that the list is a list
(Try later) Remove the blank line above the list items, render again, and see what breaks

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.10 Code chunks
R code goes in a code chunk:
```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
ice <- read_csv("data/mendota_ice.csv")
```




Starts with ```{r} and ends with ```
Lines starting with #| are chunk options
label names the chunk (use snake_case; not always required but helps when debugging)




Add this chunk just below the YAML header, save file, then render.

Open the html file again in the browser to see the changes
A setup chunk at the top loads packages and data for the whole document

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.11 Hide the messages
Your readers do not need these in your report:

the tidyverse startup messages
the column messages from read_csv()




Add one option to the setup chunk:
```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
ice <- read_csv("data/mendota_ice.csv")
```




message: false hides messages; the code still runs




Want to hide the chunk completely?

include: false runs the code but shows neither the code nor its output

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.12 Add a figure
Under ## Ice cover over time, add a chunk:
```{r}
#| label: ice_plot

ice |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = ice_days)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Winter (year it ended)", y = "Days of ice cover") +
  theme_minimal()
```



Save and render again.

Quarto runs the chunk and puts the figure right below the code
It also makes a report_files/ folder for the image; more on that in the next unit

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.13 The figure in your report













Lots of year-to-year variation
But the trend is down

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.14 Inline R
Do the work in a chunk:
```{r}
#| label: means

mean_1800s <- ice |> filter(year < 1900) |> pull(ice_days) |> mean() |> round()
mean_recent <- ice |> filter(year >= 2000) |> pull(ice_days) |> mean() |> round()
```



Then put the results in your sentences with inline R:
Before 1900, the lake averaged `r mean_1800s` days of ice.
Since 2000, it has averaged `r mean_recent`.

Backtick, the letter r, a space, then R code, then a closing backtick
Keep inline R short; do the work in a chunk


Before 1900, the lake averaged 114 days of ice. Since 2000, it has averaged 81.




Save, render, and view file again

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
section: 2.15 Render runs in a fresh session
text:
2.15 Render runs in a fresh session
In the RStudio console, run:
n_winters <- 171



Then add a sentence to report.qmd and render:
There are `r n_winters` winters in the record.



n_winters exists in your console.

So why will this fail?

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.16 The error
Error in eval(parse_only(code), envir = envir) :
  object 'n_winters' not found

Quitting from report.qmd:44-44
Execution halted



quarto render runs your code in a fresh R session.

It cannot see anything in your console
Not even chunks you ran in RStudio with the green ▶
Every object the report uses must be created in the report




This is a feature:

If it renders, anyone with your .qmd and data can rebuild it




To fix it:

Create it in the report: add n_winters <- nrow(ice) to a chunk above the sentence

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.17 Your turn







ImportantTry it




Add the means chunk and the two sentences with inline R
Add one more sentence: how many days of ice in the shortest winter on record? (Hint: min(ice$ice_days))
Render, save, and check the numbers in report.html

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.18 Your turn: what to type
Below the means chunk, your text should look like this:
Before 1900, the lake averaged `r mean_1800s` days of ice.
Since 2000, it has averaged `r mean_recent`.

The shortest winter on record had `r min(ice$ice_days)` days of ice.




Before 1900, the lake averaged 114 days of ice. Since 2000, it has averaged 81.
The shortest winter on record had 21 days of ice.




Still getting an error?

The sentences must come after the means chunk; code runs top to bottom
Delete or fix the n_winters sentence from the last demo

title: 2  Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.19 Where we are
We have:

Written a YAML header that sets the title, author, date, and format
Used markdown for headings, text, bold, and lists
Run R code in chunks, and hidden messages with chunk options
Put computed numbers in sentences with inline R
Seen that quarto render runs in a fresh session











ImportantNext up



Our report works, but it is spread across an HTML file and a folder. Next we will render it to one self-contained file and publish it online.

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.1 Two ways to share
Once your report renders, you can share it as:
We will do both in this unit.

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
a file: email it, post it on Canvas
a URL: publish it online

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.2 What render made
ls
data  report.html  report.qmd  report_files




report.html is the page
report_files/ holds the figure and the page’s styling




Email someone just report.html:

the figure and styling are missing

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.3 One self-contained file
Change format: in your YAML header:
---
title: "Ice Cover on Lake Mendota"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
---




html moves to its own line, indented under format:
YAML cares about indentation; use two spaces per level
embed-resources: true packs the figure and styling into the HTML file

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.4 Render again
quarto render report.qmd
ls
data  report.html  report.qmd




report_files/ is gone
report.html is now one file you can email or post
It is bigger (about 1.3 MB), because everything is inside it

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.5 Other formats, one flag
The same .qmd can become other formats:
quarto render report.qmd --to docx
quarto render report.qmd --to typst




docx: a Word document
typst: a PDF, with no LaTeX needed
More on Word output in the paper unit

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.6 Posit Connect Cloud
Posit Connect Cloud hosts documents online for free.

You made an account before the workshop




On the free plan, everything you publish is public:

Anyone with the link can see it
It is listed on your public profile page
This is true even if your GitHub repo is private
Never publish private or sensitive data

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.7 Publish
quarto publish posit-connect-cloud report.qmd



What happens:

Quarto renders the report on your computer
It uploads only the output
Connect Cloud never runs your code

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.8 First time only: authorize
Quarto first asks to Authorize:

Press Enter
Quarto prints an authorization code and opens your browser
Log in to Connect Cloud if asked, then approve the request




Quarto saves the authorization on your computer.

You will not need to do this again on this computer

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.9 Your report is live
When it finishes, Quarto prints the URL and opens it:
Published: https://connect.posit.cloud/your_name/content/...




Share this link with anyone
The title on Connect Cloud comes from title: in your YAML




The title is set only on the first publish.

To rename it later, use the Connect Cloud website

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.10 Update it
Change your report, then run the same command:
quarto publish posit-connect-cloud report.qmd



Quarto asks Publish update to:

The first choice is your report’s URL; press Enter
Don’t choose “Add a new destination”; that makes a second copy




How does Quarto remember the URL?

The first publish created _publish.yml next to your report
It records where report.qmd was published
Keep it, and don’t edit it

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.11 Your turn







ImportantTry it




Add a sentence with the longest winter on record (Hint: max(ice$ice_days))
Publish the update with quarto publish posit-connect-cloud report.qmd
Reload your report’s URL and find your new sentence

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.12 Where we are
We have:

Rendered the report to one self-contained HTML file
Seen that one flag switches the output to Word or PDF
Published the report to Posit Connect Cloud
Updated it at the same URL











ImportantNext up



Reports are one product. Next we will turn the same kind of document into a slide deck.

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.1 Your report is almost a deck
In the terminal, copy your report:
In slides.qmd, replace the format: lines with one line:
Render, then open slides.html in your browser:

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
cp report.qmd slides.qmd




---
title: "Ice Cover on Lake Mendota"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format: revealjs
---




revealjs is Quarto’s format for slides in a web browser
Yes, this copies your code; the paper unit comes back to that





quarto render slides.qmd

Use the arrow keys to move between slides

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.2 What you got
You changed one line, and:

The YAML header made a title slide
Each ## heading started a new slide
The code is gone: decks hide code by default




But one slide has a problem:

The figure shares its slide with your three sentences
Quarto shrinks the figure to make room for them

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.3 One idea per slide
Add a heading just above your sentences:
## The numbers

Before 1900, the lake averaged `r mean_1800s` days of ice.
Since 2000, it has averaged `r mean_recent`.




The sentences move to a new slide
The figure now has its slide to itself, and it grows to fill it




Want a new slide without a title?

Put --- on a line by itself, with blank lines around it

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.4 Bullets and pauses
Slides read better as short bullets than as sentences:
## The numbers

- Before 1900: `r mean_1800s` days of ice per winter
- Since 2000: `r mean_recent` days

. . .

- Shortest winter: `r min(ice$ice_days)` days
- Longest winter: `r max(ice$ice_days)` days



. . . on a line by itself is a pause.

The slide shows everything above it first
Press → to show the rest
Keep blank lines around it

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.5 Speaker notes
At the bottom of a slide, add:
::: {.notes}
About a month less ice than in the 1800s.
:::




Everything between ::: {.notes} and ::: is a note
Your audience doesn’t see notes




Press S for speaker view:

Your notes, a timer, and the next slide
If nothing opens, allow pop-ups for the page

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.6 Your turn







ImportantTry it




Add the ## The numbers heading, render, and check that the figure has its own slide
Turn your sentences into bullets, with a . . . pause
Add a speaker note to one slide, render, and press S

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.7 Optional: publish your deck
First, give your deck its own title in the YAML header:
title: "Less Ice on Lake Mendota"

Connect Cloud takes the title from your YAML, but only on the first publish
Your report already uses “Ice Cover on Lake Mendota”




Then publish, just like the report:
quarto publish posit-connect-cloud slides.qmd

The deck gets its own URL
_publish.yml adds a second entry, for slides.qmd

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.8 Where we are
We have:

Turned the report into a slide deck by changing format:
Split slides with ## headings, so each idea gets its own slide
Added bullets, pauses, and speaker notes











ImportantNext up



A project often goes from report, to slides for a conference talk, to a paper. Next we will write the paper.

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.1 What a paper needs
A paper needs things a report doesn’t:
And usually a Word file:

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
Citations and a reference list in a required style
Numbered figures and tables you can refer to in the text
An abstract
No visible code






Co-authors edit it with track changes
Many journals ask for .docx

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.2 Start from your report
In the terminal, in your mendota_ice folder:
cp report.qmd paper.qmd




cp copies a file: first the original, then the new name
paper.qmd starts with everything your report has




Copying is fine for today, but now the same code lives in three files: report, slides, and paper.

Change one, and you must remember to change the other
The DRY unit shows how to keep the code in one place

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.3 A paper’s YAML header
Replace the YAML header at the top of paper.qmd:
---
title: "Ice Cover on Lake Mendota"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
abstract: |
  Lake Mendota freezes for fewer days each winter than it did in the 1800s.
  We summarize more than 170 years of ice records.
format: docx
execute:
  echo: false
---




abstract: | starts a block; the indented lines below it are the abstract
format: docx builds a Word document
execute: echo: false hides all code; readers see only the results
No embed-resources needed; a Word file always holds its own figures

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.4 Render to Word
quarto render paper.qmd



Quarto writes paper.docx next to your .qmd.

Open it in Word (or Google Docs, or LibreOffice)




You should see:

The abstract under the title
Your sections, sentences, and figure
No code




On Windows, close paper.docx in Word before you render again.

Word locks open files, so Quarto can’t replace it

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.5 Citations need a .bib file
You downloaded refs.bib during setup. It holds one entry (shortened here):
@dataset{magnuson2026,
  author    = {Magnuson, J. J. and Carpenter, S. R. and Stanley, E. H.},
  title     = {{North Temperate Lakes LTER}: Ice Duration - ...},
  year      = {2026},
  publisher = {Environmental Data Initiative},
  doi       = {10.6073/pasta/6a95bee73799927cbafbf87393be7038},
  ...
}




magnuson2026 is the citation key; you cite the source with it
Get entries from Google Scholar (Cite → BibTeX), a journal’s “Export citation” link, or Zotero




Point your paper to the file; add to the YAML header:
bibliography: refs.bib

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.6 Citation style
Quarto’s default style is Chicago author-date.

For APA, add one more line to the YAML header:

bibliography: refs.bib
csl: apa.csl



A CSL (Citation Style Language) file describes one style.

You downloaded apa.csl during setup, next to refs.bib
Thousands of styles, including many journals, are at https://www.zotero.org/styles
For another style, download its .csl file into your repo and change the csl: line

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.7 Cite a source
In your Background section, add a citation to the first sentence:
Lake Mendota has been watched for ice since the **1850s** [@magnuson2026].






You type
Quarto writes




[@magnuson2026]
(Magnuson et al., 2026)


@magnuson2026
Magnuson et al. (2026)






At the very end of paper.qmd, add a heading:
## References

Quarto puts the reference list there, formatted in APA

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.8 Number the figure
Change the figure chunk’s label and add a caption:
```{r}
#| label: fig-ice_days
#| fig-cap: "Days of ice cover on Lake Mendota, by winter."

ice |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = ice_days)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Winter (year it ended)", y = "Days of ice cover") +
  theme_minimal()
```



Then refer to it in a sentence:
Ice cover has declined since the 1850s (@fig-ice_days).

The label must start with fig-; Quarto requires that hyphen (the rest stays snake_case)
Quarto numbers the figure and writes “Figure 1” for you

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.11 Your turn: check your paper
In paper.docx, look for (Magnuson et al., 2026), Figure 1, Table 1, and the reference list.



A typo doesn’t stop the render.

Quarto prints a WARNING in the terminal and keeps going
Read the render output, not just the Word file











You see
Fix




(magnuson?)

?@fig-ice_days

Code in the Word file
Check the indentation of echo: false under execute:

title: 5  Writing a Paper
section: 5.12 Word and PDF from one render
text:
5.12 Word and PDF from one render

format:
  docx: default
  typst:
    citeproc: true



quarto render paper.qmd now makes both paper.docx and paper.pdf.

default means “no extra options for this format”
Typst makes the PDF, with no LaTeX needed




Why citeproc: true?

Typst formats citations itself, and its APA output differs a little from Word’s
This tells it to use the same citation engine as the Word file

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.13 Where we are
We have:

Turned the report into a paper with a few YAML changes
Cited a source, with a reference list in APA style
Numbered a figure and a table, and referred to them in the text
Rendered to Word (and PDF)











ImportantWhere to go next



The Advanced units in the book (no slides) pick up from here.

Start with Git: commit what you built today
Then keep editing your own report, slides, and paper, and render them to see each new feature
Topics: more markdown, chunk options and figures, tables, slide formatting, YAML in depth, Quarto projects, and keeping one copy of your code for all three

title: 6  Git with Quarto Projects
text:
6.1 What’s in your repo now
In the workshop, we built a report, a slide deck, and a paper in your mendota_ice repo, but we never committed any of it. That was on purpose. Rendering fills your repo with files that Quarto makes, and most of them don’t belong in Git. This unit sorts out which files to commit and which to ignore, then commits and pushes your work.
The same rules apply to any repo where you use Quarto.
In your mendota_ice folder, run:
If you finished all the workshop units, you will see something like this:
Your list may be a little different. For example, you will only have paper.pdf and .quarto/ if you also rendered the paper to PDF with Typst.

title: 6  Git with Quarto Projects
text:
git status

On branch main
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    .quarto/
    _publish.yml
    apa.csl
    data/
    paper.docx
    paper.pdf
    paper.qmd
    refs.bib
    report.html
    report.qmd
    slides.html
    slides.qmd
    slides_files/

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

title: 6  Git with Quarto Projects
section: 6.2 Commit what you write, ignore what Quarto makes
text:
6.2 Commit what you write, ignore what Quarto makes
The rule of thumb is simple:

Commit the files you write: your .qmd files and the inputs they need (data, references, citation style).
Ignore the files Quarto makes: anything quarto render can rebuild.

Rendered output doesn’t belong in Git for several reasons:

You can always rebuild it. Anyone with your source files can run quarto render and get the same output.
It changes every time you render. Our report uses date: today, so report.html changes every day you render it, even if nothing else did. Those changes clutter every commit.
It’s often binary. Git can’t show you what changed inside a .docx or .pdf, and it can’t merge two versions of one. If two people change the same Word file, someone has to pick one version.
It’s big. With embed-resources: true, report.html holds the figure and all the supporting code, so it’s over a megabyte. Git keeps every version you commit, forever.
It can go stale. A committed report.html may no longer match report.qmd, and nothing warns you.

You share output in other ways: publish it (as we did with Connect Cloud), or send the Word file to a co-author.
Here is how each file in your repo sorts out:








File
What it is
Commit?




report.qmd, slides.qmd, paper.qmd
Your source documents
Yes


data/mendota_ice.csv
Data the documents read
Yes


refs.bib
References the paper cites
Yes


apa.csl
Citation style for the paper
Yes


_publish.yml
Where each document is published (see below)
Yes


.gitignore
What Git should ignore
Yes


report.html, slides.html
Rendered HTML
No


slides_files/
Images and code the HTML deck needs
No


paper.docx, paper.pdf
Rendered Word and PDF
No


.quarto/
Quarto’s scratch folder
No



Committing data is fine here because the file is small and public. For large or private data, think twice; that’s a topic for another day.

6.2.1 Where the extra folders come from

slides_files/: a revealjs deck needs supporting files (the figure, plus the code that runs the slides). Quarto puts them in a folder named after the document. The report has no report_files/ folder because embed-resources: true packs everything into report.html.
.quarto/: Quarto’s own working folder. For single documents like ours, it appears when you render to PDF with Typst. Quarto projects (folders with a _quarto.yml file) always have one.

If a render fails partway, Quarto can leave intermediate files behind, such as a paper_files/ folder or a paper.typ file. The next successful render cleans them up.

title: 6  Git with Quarto Projects
text:
6.3 Update your .gitignore
Your repo already has a .gitignore: the R template you chose on GitHub. It covers R’s clutter (.Rhistory, .RData, .Rproj.user/) and keeps secrets like .Renviron and .env out of Git. It knows nothing about Quarto.
Open .gitignore in RStudio, add these lines at the end, and save:
# Quarto
/.quarto/
*_files/
*.html
*.docx
*.pdf
What each line does:

/.quarto/ ignores Quarto’s scratch folder. The leading / means “only at the top of the repo”.
*_files/ ignores any folder whose name ends in _files, like slides_files/.
*.html, *.docx, and *.pdf ignore rendered output anywhere in the repo.

These patterns are broad on purpose, so new documents are covered without editing .gitignore again. If you ever do want to commit one of these files, say a PDF of a published article you keep in a literature/ folder, add an exception line that starts with !:
!literature/*.pdf
Now check your work:
git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
    modified:   .gitignore

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    _publish.yml
    apa.csl
    data/
    paper.qmd
    refs.bib
    report.qmd
    slides.qmd

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
The output files are gone from the list. Only the files you wrote are left.

6.3.1 Checking what Git ignores
Two commands help when you aren’t sure. To list ignored files (marked !!):
git status --short --ignored
 M .gitignore
?? _publish.yml
?? apa.csl
?? data/
?? paper.qmd
?? refs.bib
?? report.qmd
?? slides.qmd
!! .quarto/
!! paper.docx
!! paper.pdf
!! report.html
!! slides.html
!! slides_files/
To see which line of .gitignore ignores a file:
git check-ignore -v slides.html slides_files
.gitignore:55:*.html    slides.html
.gitignore:54:*_files/  slides_files
Your line numbers may differ. If git check-ignore prints nothing for a file, Git is not ignoring it.

title: 6  Git with Quarto Projects
text:
6.4 Commit and push
With a good .gitignore in place, git add . is safe: it stages everything Git doesn’t ignore. Still, check what you staged before you commit.
git add .
git status
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
    modified:   .gitignore
    new file:   _publish.yml
    new file:   apa.csl
    new file:   data/mendota_ice.csv
    new file:   paper.qmd
    new file:   refs.bib
    new file:   report.qmd
    new file:   slides.qmd
Only source files. Commit and push:
git commit -m "Add report, slides, and paper"
git push
From now on, the routine is the same as any other repo: edit your .qmd files, render to check them, then commit the .qmd changes. Rendering never adds anything new for Git to track.






ImportantYour turn




Add a sentence to report.qmd and render it
Run git status: only report.qmd should show as modified
Commit and push the change

title: 6  Git with Quarto Projects
text:
6.5 If you already committed output
.gitignore only affects files Git isn’t tracking yet. If you committed report.html before adding *.html to .gitignore, Git keeps tracking it, and every render shows it as modified:
 M report.html
 M report.qmd
To stop tracking a file without deleting it from your computer, use git rm --cached, then commit:
git rm --cached report.html
git commit -m "Stop tracking report.html"
report.html stays on your computer, and from now on .gitignore applies to it. For a folder, add -r: git rm -r --cached slides_files.
Older versions of the file stay in your Git history. That’s fine for a small report. Removing files from history is possible but disruptive, and you rarely need it.

title: 6  Git with Quarto Projects
text:
6.6 Commit _publish.yml
_publish.yml is the file quarto publish writes the first time you publish a document. It records where each document went:
- source: report.qmd
  posit-connect-cloud:
    - id: 01a1c082-...
      url: https://connect.posit.cloud/your_name/content/01a1c082-...
Commit it. It’s what makes quarto publish offer to update your existing report instead of creating a new copy at a new URL. With it in your repo, you can republish from another computer, or a teammate can, and the URL your readers have keeps working.
It holds only IDs and URLs, not your login. Quarto keeps your Connect Cloud credentials on your computer, outside the repo, so _publish.yml is safe to commit even to a public repo.
Two tips:

To publish a document to a new URL (for example, so a new title takes effect), delete its entry from _publish.yml, then publish again. Delete the old copy on the Connect Cloud website if you no longer want it.
To start over completely, delete the whole file. Don’t leave it empty: Quarto can’t read an empty _publish.yml, so it stops recording where you publish.

title: 6  Git with Quarto Projects
text:
6.7 When you add a _quarto.yml
Our repo has no _quarto.yml, so it isn’t a Quarto project. Each document renders on its own. If you later turn a folder into a project (for a website, a book, or to share settings across documents; see Chapter 12), a few things change for Git:

Quarto edits .gitignore for you. When you render a project inside a Git repo, Quarto adds /.quarto/ and **/*.quarto_ipynb to .gitignore if they aren’t already there. (*.quarto_ipynb files are temporary files from rendering documents that run Python through Jupyter.) It doesn’t do this for single documents like ours, which is why we added /.quarto/ by hand.
Websites and books render to an output folder: _site/ for websites and _book/ for books. Quarto does not add these to .gitignore. If you publish with quarto publish, add them yourself.
The R template ignores docs/. If you publish a website with GitHub Pages from a docs/ folder, that output does need to be committed, so delete the docs/ line from .gitignore.
Commit _freeze/. If your project uses freeze, Quarto saves the results of your code in a _freeze/ folder and reuses them instead of rerunning the code. The Quarto documentation recommends committing it, so others can render the project without setting up your whole computing environment.

title: 6  Git with Quarto Projects
text:
6.8 Summary
For a repo of Quarto documents like mendota_ice, add this to the .gitignore you got from GitHub’s R template:
# Quarto
/.quarto/
*_files/
*.html
*.docx
*.pdf
Then:

Commit your .qmd files, the data, references, and citation style they read, _publish.yml, and .gitignore.
Ignore everything quarto render makes. Share output by publishing it instead.
If you committed output by mistake, git rm --cached stops tracking it.
In Quarto projects, let Quarto manage /.quarto/, ignore _site/ or _book/ unless you publish from them, and commit _freeze/.

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.1 Text formatting
In the workshop, you used the basics of markdown: headings, paragraphs, bold, bulleted lists, and the blank lines that hold them together. This unit covers the rest of the markdown you are likely to use: more text formatting, numbered and nested lists, links, images, footnotes, tables you type by hand, math, and callout boxes.
Everything here works in reports, slide decks, and papers. Where an output format handles something differently, we say so.
Each example shows what you type, followed by what you get (in a green box). Try them in your own report.qmd and render to see them for yourself.
If you committed your work in Chapter 6, experiment freely. If you make a mess of report.qmd, git restore report.qmd takes it back to your last commit.
You type:
You get:
Inline code (text between single backticks) is only formatting: it shows the text in a code font, so readers can tell ice_days is a column name. Quarto doesn’t run it. Inline R code, which does run, starts with the letter r right after the first backtick, as you saw in the workshop.

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
Lake Mendota is *frozen* for **fewer days** than it was in the 1800s.
Some winters it ***barely*** freezes.

A winter now averages ~~114~~ 81 days of ice.
Water is H~2~O, and the lake holds about 5 × 10^11^ liters.
Use the `ice_days` column.


Lake Mendota is frozen for fewer days than it was in the 1800s. Some winters it barely freezes.
A winter now averages 114 81 days of ice. Water is H2O, and the lake holds about 5 × 1011 liters. Use the ice_days column.








You type
You get




*italic*
italic


**bold**
bold


***bold italic***
bold italic


~~strikethrough~~
strikethrough


H~2~O (subscript)
H2O


10^11^ (superscript)
1011


`code` (inline code)
code

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.2 Paragraphs and line breaks
Markdown joins lines that have no blank line between them into one paragraph. That’s why the two sentences about averages in your report, typed on two lines, appear as one paragraph.

To start a new paragraph, leave a blank line.
To break a line without starting a new paragraph (useful for addresses or poems), end the line with a backslash (\).

You type:
Lake Mendota\
Madison, Wisconsin\
United States
You get:

Lake Mendota
Madison, Wisconsin
United States

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.3 Numbered and nested lists
Numbered lists use a number and a period. Quarto does the counting, so you can type 1. for every item; adding an item in the middle never means renumbering by hand. The first number sets where the list starts.
To nest a list inside another, indent the inner items so they line up with the text of the item above: two spaces under a - item, three spaces under a 1. item. Four spaces works under both.
You type:
To update your report:

1. Edit `report.qmd`
1. Render it
    - Fix any errors
    - Render again
1. Publish the update
You get:

To update your report:

Edit report.qmd
Render it

Fix any errors
Render again

Publish the update


As with bulleted lists, leave a blank line before a numbered list.
Two numbered lists in a row, separated only by a blank line, become one list. Put a line of text between them to keep them apart.

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.4 Links
You type:
The data are from the [Environmental Data Initiative](https://doi.org/10.6073/pasta/6a95bee73799927cbafbf87393be7038).
Learn more at <https://quarto.org>.
You get:

The data are from the Environmental Data Initiative. Learn more at https://quarto.org.


[text](url) makes the text a link.
<url> shows the address itself as a link. Without the angle brackets, the address is plain text, not a link.







ImportantYour turn



In your report.qmd:

Put one word in italics and add a link to the data source in your Background section
Turn the two bullets about the record into a numbered list, and nest a bullet under one of them
Render and check the result

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.5 Images
An image looks like a link with an exclamation mark in front:
![Lake Mendota in January.](images/mendota_winter.jpg){width=60%}

The path (images/mendota_winter.jpg) is relative to your .qmd file, just like the path to your data.
{width=60%} is optional. It sets the image’s width as a share of the page.
When the image sits in a paragraph by itself, the text in the square brackets becomes a caption, and Quarto treats the image as a figure.

The caption is not alt text, the description that screen readers read aloud. Add alt text with fig-alt:
![Lake Mendota in January.](images/mendota_winter.jpg){width=60% fig-alt="Snow-covered ice on Lake Mendota, with the Capitol in the distance."}
For an image with no caption, leave the square brackets empty: ![](images/mendota_winter.jpg){fig-alt="..."}.
With embed-resources: true, the image is packed into your HTML file, so you can publish the report as before. Word and PDF files always hold their own images.
This is for image files, like photos or diagrams. For plots you make in R, use a code chunk instead; Chapter 8 covers how to size and caption them.

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.6 Block quotes
Start a line with > to set it off as a quotation. For example, to quote the rule as the story from the workshop tells it:
You type:
> The lake is frozen if you can't row a boat from Picnic Point to Maple Bluff.
You get:


The lake is frozen if you can’t row a boat from Picnic Point to Maple Bluff.

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text: Records for 1852-53 and 1853-54 are incomplete, and 1854-55 is missing.↩︎

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.8 Tables you type by hand
For a small table of numbers you already know, you can type it as a pipe table:
| Winter  | Days of ice | Record   |
|:--------|------------:|:--------:|
| 1880-81 |         161 | Longest  |
| 2001-02 |          21 | Shortest |

: Record winters on Lake Mendota. {#tbl-records}
You get:




Table 7.1: Record winters on Lake Mendota.





Winter
Days of ice
Record




1880-81
161
Longest


2001-02
21
Shortest








| separates the columns. The columns don’t have to line up in your source, but lining them up makes the table easier to read and edit.
The second line separates the header from the rows. Colons set alignment: :--- left, ---: right, :---: centered. Right-align numbers.
The line starting with : after the table is its caption. It’s optional.
{#tbl-records} gives the table a label, so you can refer to it as @tbl-records, just as you did for the table in your paper. Here, @tbl-records becomes “Table 7.1”.

Hand-typed tables are for fixed content. If the numbers come from your data, make the table with code, so it updates when the data change. Chapter 9 covers that.

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.9 Math
Quarto writes math in LaTeX notation, which is the standard for equations.

Put math inside a sentence between single dollar signs: $...$.
Put an equation on its own line between double dollar signs: $$...$$.

You type:
The mean of $n$ winters is $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i$.

$$
\bar{x}_{\text{recent}} - \bar{x}_{\text{1800s}} = 81 - 114 = -33
$$
You get:

The mean of \(n\) winters is \(\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\).
\[
\bar{x}_{\text{recent}} - \bar{x}_{\text{1800s}} = 81 - 114 = -33
\]

Math works in HTML, in Word (as real, editable Word equations), and in PDF.
A few LaTeX pieces cover most needs:







You type
You get




x^2, x_i
\(x^2\), \(x_i\)


\frac{a}{b}
\(\frac{a}{b}\)


\bar{x}, \hat{\beta}
\(\bar{x}\), \(\hat{\beta}\)


\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\)


\sqrt{x}
\(\sqrt{x}\)


\alpha, \mu, \sigma
\(\alpha\), \(\mu\), \(\sigma\)


\le, \ge, \ne, \approx
\(\le\), \(\ge\), \(\ne\), \(\approx\)



Dollar amounts usually come out fine: Quarto only treats $...$ as math when there’s no space just inside the dollar signs. If one ever turns into math by mistake, type \$ for a plain dollar sign.

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.10 Callouts
A callout is a colored box that sets off a note, tip, or warning. It starts with ::: {.callout-note} and ends with :::, each on its own line:
::: {.callout-note}
## About the data
A winter counts in the year it ends: winter 1855-56 is 1856.
:::
You get:







NoteAbout the data



A winter counts in the year it ends: winter 1855-56 is 1856.




There are five types: callout-note, callout-tip, callout-important, callout-warning, and callout-caution. Each has its own color.
A heading on the first line inside becomes the callout’s title. You can also write the title as an option: ::: {.callout-warning title="Check your paths"}.
In HTML, add collapse="true" to show only the title until the reader clicks it: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}. Word and PDF show the whole callout.

Callouts work in HTML, Word, PDF, and slides.






ImportantYour turn



In your report.qmd:

Add a footnote to your Background section
Add the record-winters table above, and refer to it in a sentence with @tbl-records
Add a callout-note that explains how a winter’s year is counted
Render and check the result

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.11 Comments
Text between <!-- and --> is a comment. It doesn’t appear in your rendered document, so it’s handy for notes to yourself or for switching off a paragraph without deleting it:
<!-- TODO: add the 2026-27 winter when the data are updated -->
In RStudio, select some lines and press Ctrl+Shift+C (Cmd+Shift+C on a Mac) to comment them out or back in.






WarningComments are hidden, not removed



Word and PDF files leave comments out completely. An HTML file keeps them in its source code, so anyone who opens View Source on your published report can read them. Don’t put anything private in a comment.

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.12 Escaping special characters
Characters like *, _, #, and $ have special meanings in markdown. To show one as a plain character, put a backslash in front of it.
You type:
Multiply 3 \* 4 and see \*this\*, not *this*.
You get:

Multiply 3 * 4 and see *this*, not this.

Often you don’t need to: a * with spaces on both sides, as in 3 * 4, stays a plain *.

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.13 Horizontal rules
Three dashes on a line by themselves, with blank lines around them, draw a horizontal line across a report. You have seen --- do two other jobs: it starts and ends the YAML header, and in a slide deck it starts a new slide.

title: 7  Advanced Markdown
text:
7.14 Divs and spans
Callouts are one example of a general markdown pattern that you will see more of:

A div wraps a block of content: ::: with a class in braces opens it, and ::: closes it. Callouts, the speaker notes in your slide deck (::: {.notes}), and slide columns are all divs.
A span wraps a few words inside a sentence: square brackets, then a class in braces.

You type:
This word is [underlined]{.underline}, and these are [Small Caps]{.smallcaps}.
You get:

This word is underlined, and these are Small Caps.

Chapter 10 uses divs and spans to lay out slides.
